title: Wax Fruit Models: Apples, Oranges, and Grapes
description: Wax fruit models are the classic beginner's display piece: an apple, an orange, and a cluster of grapes, each modeled in beeswax so faithfully that shoppers reach for them before they remember the bowl is a display. The maker works from real fruit, taking molds or modeling by eye, coloring in thin washes, and finishing with a matte skin that catches light the way real peel does. Apple and orange bodies in this record use pure beeswax, while the grape stems use a labeled blend of 80 percent beeswax and 20 percent microcrystalline wax, never passed off as pure beeswax. These are display models made with beeswax. They are not food, they are not edible, and they must never be eaten.
model_subject: Wax apples, oranges, and grapes for fruit-bowl and shop displays
materials: Pure beeswax (100% beeswax, melting point about 62-64 C) for the apple and orange bodies
Display blend, labeled: 80% beeswax, 20% microcrystalline wax, for the grape cluster stems and leaves
Powdered mineral pigments for coloring (red, orange, green, purple)
Silicone molds taken from real fruit, or hand-modeled forms
Fine brushes, a warm spatula, and a clear matte sealant
method: Warm the beeswax gently in a double boiler until it flows, never over an open flame.
Pour or brush the wax into silicone molds taken from real apples and oranges, then let each layer cool before adding the next.
Model grapes one small sphere at a time and join them on a wax stem, building the cluster from the top down.
Color each model while the wax is still slightly warm, layering thin washes so the color sits in the skin texture.
Add a stem, a leaf, and a soft matte finish, then check the model against real fruit in daylight.
realism: Press a real apple skin lightly against the cooling wax to transfer its fine pores, and shade one side warmer where the sun would have ripened it. A tiny browned spot near the stem sells the realism at shop-window distance.
safety: NOT FOOD: display models made with beeswax are not food and must never be eaten. Keep display fruit out of direct sun and away from radiators, since beeswax softens near 62 C.
care: Keep display fruit out of direct sun and away from radiators, since beeswax softens near 62 C. Dust with a soft dry brush, never with water and soap, and store each piece in tissue in a cool cupboard. These are display models made with beeswax. They are not food, they are not edible, and they must never be eaten.
variations: A single perfect apple for a classroom display
A mixed orchard bowl with apples, oranges, and grapes
Oversized fruit for a market-stall window

title: Wax Vegetable Models: Carrots, Cucumbers, and Tomatoes

The maker shapes each vegetable from its real geometry, colors it in sun-and-shade layers, and finishes the surface details that the eye checks first. Carrot and tomato bodies here use pure beeswax, while cucumber skins use a labeled blend of 75 percent beeswax and 25 percent microcrystalline wax. These are display models made with beeswax. They are not food, they are not edible, and they must never be eaten.
model_subject: Wax carrots, cucumbers, tomatoes, and leafy greens for market displays

Display blend, labeled: 75% beeswax, 25% microcrystalline wax, for cucumber skins that need a firmer edge

method: Model each vegetable around its real shape: a tapered cone for the carrot, a long cylinder for the cucumber, a slightly flattened sphere for the tomato.

Color in layers, darkest in the creases and lightest on the sun-facing side.
Add surface detail last: carrot rings, cucumber bumps, and the star scar on a tomato top.
realism: Carrot ring ridges are scored with a blunt tool while the wax is firm but not cold, and cucumber bumps are pressed with a real cucumber half rolled across the surface. Leaf veins are drawn with a warm needle.

care: Store vegetables upright in a cool, dry case, out of sunlight and away from heat above 40 C. title: Wax Savory Dish Models: The Sampuru Technique
description: The Japanese sampuru tradition builds whole plated dishes in wax so faithfully that a restaurant window can show its menu without cooking a single plate. The maker studies the real dish from the window's viewpoint, models each component separately, pours sauces as warm wax so they pool naturally, and sets garnishes with tweezers. This record teaches the technique, and its subjects stay inside the suite's world: cheese-and-vegetable platters, bread-and-butter service, and milk-pudding cups with honey drizzle in wax. Plated dishes here use a labeled blend of 70 percent beeswax and 30 percent microcrystalline wax, with pure beeswax for butter and cream garnishes. These are display models made with beeswax. They are not food, they are not edible, and they must never be eaten.
model_subject: Wax savory dish models in the Japanese sampuru technique, with milk, honey, dairy, bakery, fruit, and vegetable subjects
materials: Display blend, labeled: 70% beeswax, 30% microcrystalline wax, for plated dishes that must hold shape under case lights
Pure beeswax (100% beeswax) for butter pats, cream dollops, and soft garnishes
Food-color mineral pigments matched to each dish
Real plates, bowls, and serving dishes as molds and bases
Fine brushes, tweezers, and a warm needle for garnish work
method: Study the real dish first and photograph it from the angle the window will show, since sampuru models are built for one viewpoint.
Model each component separately: the plate base, the main item, the sauce or glaze, and the garnish, then assemble while the wax is warm.
Pour sauces as thin warm wax so they pool and drip the way a real sauce does, and set garnishes with tweezers.
Finish with a light gloss on wet-looking foods and a matte finish on dry ones, and check the plate under case lighting.
realism: This is a technique record: the sampuru craft of building a whole plated dish in wax, with the suite's own subjects as the models. In this suite the savory plates are dairy, bakery, and vegetable plates, such as a cheese-and-vegetable platter, butter pats with bread, and milk-pudding cups, never slaughter-derived dishes presented as suite foods. The realism test is the sauce: it must look poured, not painted.
safety: NOT FOOD: display models made with beeswax are not food and must never be eaten. Plated models are the most handled pieces, so keep them in a closed case and lift by the plate, never by a garnish.
care: Plated models are the most handled pieces, so keep them in a closed case and lift by the plate, never by a garnish. Dust dry, and keep below 25 C. These are display models made with beeswax. They are not food, they are not edible, and they must never be eaten.
variations: A cheese-and-vegetable platter in the sampuru style
A bread-and-butter service plate
A milk-pudding cup trio with honey drizzle in wax

title: Wax Model Making: Molds, Coloring, and Finishing
description: Wax model making is the craft behind every other record in this pair: masters, silicone and plaster molds, wax pouring, coloring, and finishing. The maker finishes the master fully, since molds copy flaws faithfully, brushes silicone in thin layers or pours plaster in keyed halves, pours wax just above its melting point, and colors in two stages, body color mixed in and surface color washed on. Production castings here use blends labeled with their exact beeswax percentage, never presented as pure beeswax. These are display models made with beeswax. They are not food, they are not edible, and they must never be eaten.
model_subject: Wax model making: silicone and plaster molds, coloring, and finishing
materials: Pure beeswax (100% beeswax) for master models and fine castings

Mineral pigments, powdered and paste, for coloring wax
Brushes, spatulas, a double boiler, and a thermometer
method: Make the master first, from clay or a real object, and finish it fully, since every mold copies the master's flaws.
Brush silicone over the master in thin layers for flexible molds, or pour plaster in two halves for rigid molds, with keys so the halves align.
Warm wax to just above its melting point, about 70 C, and pour slowly to avoid bubbles, tapping the mold to release trapped air.
Color by mixing pigment into warm wax for body color, then paint surface color in thin washes after the casting cools.
Finish by trimming seams with a warm knife, polishing with a soft cloth, and sealing with a thin matte or gloss coat as the subject needs.
realism: Mold choice decides the finish: silicone captures fine skin texture and releases easily, while plaster is cheaper for large simple shapes but needs release agent and captures less detail. Shrinkage of about 1 to 2 percent is normal and is allowed for by making the master slightly oversize.
safety: NOT FOOD: display models made with beeswax are not food and must never be eaten. Molds live longest in a cool, dry place, silicone flat and plaster dry; never stack heavy molds on silicone.
care: Molds live longest in a cool, dry place, silicone flat and plaster dry; never stack heavy molds on silicone. Keep all wax work away from open flame, and melt wax only in a double boiler. These are display models made with beeswax. They are not food, they are not edible, and they must never be eaten.

title: Wax Model Repair and Care
description: Wax model repair and care keeps a display alive for decades: dry dusting only, gentle warming to reshape bent pieces, matched wax patches for chips, warmed joins for breaks, and cool, closed-case storage with tissue between pieces. The maker records each model's blend on its display card, since a patch must match the original blend to age and color the same way. Heat is the great enemy throughout, since beeswax softens near 62 C. These are display models made with beeswax. They are not food, they are not edible, and they must never be eaten.
model_subject: Wax model repair and care: cleaning, storage, and heat warnings
materials: Pure beeswax (100% beeswax) for patching and rebuilding damaged areas
Display blends, labeled with their exact composition, for patching blended models
Soft brushes, lint-free cloths, and tissue paper for storage
A hair dryer on its lowest setting and a warm spatula for reshaping
Mineral pigments matched to the original model for touch-ups
method: Dust first with a soft dry brush, working from the top down, and never use water, soap, or solvents on a wax model.
For a bent piece, warm it gently with a hair dryer on its lowest setting until it moves, reshape it, and let it cool undisturbed.
For a chip, warm a matching wax patch, press it into the chip, trim with a warm knife when cool, and touch up the color in thin washes.
For a broken piece, warm both faces, join them, support the join until cool, and reinforce from behind with a hidden wax fillet.
Store models in tissue in closed cases in a cool room below 25 C, with wax never touching wax.
realism: Repairs must match the original blend: patching a blended model with pure beeswax changes how the patch ages and colors, so record each model's blend on its display card. Heat is the great enemy: beeswax softens near 62 C, and a model left in a hot car or sunny window will slump beyond repair.
safety: NOT FOOD: display models made with beeswax are not food and must never be eaten. Store every model below 25 C, out of sun, away from radiators and hot cars, and out of reach of children who might mistake a realistic model for food.

title: Wax Model Safety: Food-Grade Wax Versus Display Wax
description: Wax model safety rests on one separation: food-grade beeswax, E901, is the only wax that touches real food, while display wax, with its pigments, blends, wire armatures, and sealants, never touches anything edible. The maker keeps the two waxes in separate labeled containers, never shares tools between them, labels every display model NOT FOOD in plain words, and never presents paraffin, microcrystalline wax, or carnauba wax as beeswax. A display model is never food, however realistic it looks. These are display models made with beeswax. They are not food, they are not edible, and they must never be eaten.
model_subject: Wax model safety: food-grade wax versus display wax, separation, and labeling
materials: Food-grade beeswax (E901) for any wax that touches real food, such as cheese coatings and fruit coatings
Display beeswax and labeled display blends for models only, never for food contact
Mineral pigments rated safe for display use, kept separate from food-grade colorings
Display cards and labels stating NOT FOOD in plain words on every model
Separate tools, containers, and storage for food-grade wax and display wax
method: Keep food-grade beeswax (E901) and display wax in separate labeled containers, on separate shelves, and never share tools between them.
Label every display model NOT FOOD on its display card and, where the model allows, on its base, in plain words a child can understand.
Never use a display model as a food container, a serving plate for real food, or a mold for real food, since display pigments and blends are not food-grade.
Never present paraffin, microcrystalline wax, or carnauba wax as beeswax: every blend is labeled with its actual composition.
Teach every person who handles the display the separation rule: food-grade wax touches food, display wax touches nothing edible.
realism: Separation is the whole safety system. Real food coatings use food-grade beeswax, E901, and nothing else touches food. Display models may contain pigments, microcrystalline wax, carnauba wax, wire armatures, and sealants that are not food-grade, which is why no display model is ever food, however realistic it looks.
safety: NOT FOOD: display models made with beeswax are not food and must never be eaten. Display models must be labeled NOT FOOD, stored away from real food, and kept out of reach of small children, since a realistic wax apple or cake can tempt a child to bite it.
care: Display models must be labeled NOT FOOD, stored away from real food, and kept out of reach of small children, since a realistic wax apple or cake can tempt a child to bite it. These are display models made with beeswax. They are not food, they are not edible, and they must never be eaten.

title: Wax Display Craft History: Sampuru and the Shop Window
description: Wax display craft history begins in the early twentieth century, when Japanese restaurants began showing their menus as wax dishes in their windows, and makers developed the sampuru craft of building whole plated dishes for a single viewpoint. The craft spread to bakery cases, dairy counters, and cafe windows, and its techniques changed along the way, silicone molds and labeled blends joining hand modeling and wash coloring, while its test never changed: a passerby must read the dish at a glance and understand it is a display. These are display models made with beeswax. They are not food, they are not edible, and they must never be eaten.

method: Study the tradition first: Japanese food models, called sampuru, grew in the early twentieth century as restaurants showed their menus in windows, and makers learned to build whole dishes in wax for a single viewpoint.
Learn the old hand skills before the modern shortcuts: modeling by eye, coloring in washes, and finishing by hand, since those skills decide whether a model reads as food or as plastic.
Follow the craft into the modern shop window: bakery cases, dairy counters, and cafe windows adopted the same techniques for bread, cheese, cakes, and drinks.
Keep the tradition honest: a modern model may use new blends and silicone molds, but its blend is labeled, its viewpoint is planned, and its display card states plainly that it is a model.

The techniques changed, silicone replacing some plaster and blends replacing some pure wax, but the test never changed: a passerby must read the dish at a glance and understand it is a display.
